draft.title: Measures beyond GDP
card: Real GDP per person measures income only. Some measures combine income with other things that shape how well people live, to give a fuller picture of living standards.
The Human Development Index (HDI) combines three parts: health (life expectancy at birth), education (years of schooling) and income per person.
Each part is scored, and the scores are combined into one number between 0 and 1. A number closer to 1 means higher human development.
Two countries with the same income per person can have different HDI scores. The country with better health and education scores higher.
draft.remember: HDI adds health and education to income, so it gives a fuller picture than income alone.

a.q: Which set of three parts is combined to make the Human Development Index?
opts: Income, life expectancy and years of schooling
Life expectancy, safety and leisure time
Years of schooling, exports and real GDP
a.why: The HDI combines income per person with health, shown by life expectancy, and education, shown by years of schooling. The set with unemployment and inflation names real economic indicators, but they are not parts of the HDI.
a.clue: The HDI adds health and education to income.

b.q: Country P and Country Q have the same income per person. Country P has a higher life expectancy and more years of schooling. What is the likely result for their HDI scores?
opts: Country P scores higher than Country Q
Country Q scores higher than Country P
They score the same, because income is equal
They cannot be compared without real GDP growth
b.why: The HDI includes health and education as well as income. With income equal, Country P's better health and education give it a higher score. Equal income does not mean equal HDI, because income is only one of three parts.
b.clue: Equal income removes one part. Look at what is left.

a.best: Income, life expectancy and years of schooling

b.best: Country P scores higher than Country Q

check.summary: No problems found. The card simplifies the HDI education measure to 'years of schooling' (the UNDP uses mean and expected years) and its income measure to 'income per person' (it uses GNI per person), which is reasonable for Year 11.
